title: Atlassian — Collaborative Kanban Board Rehearsal
briefing: A P40 candidate’s June 29, 2025 report describes whiteboarding a Trello-like board: component architecture, state management, drag-and-drop, caching, and optimistic updates. Design a board where users create cards, move them between columns, and see teammates’ changes. This exercise adapts a public candidate report; company attribution and interview details are not independently verified. The practice constraints and follow-ups are Codematica additions. Use your own timer and drawing tool: 45 minutes designing, 10 minutes handling follow-ups, and 5 minutes reviewing. No coding is required. Your design is not automatically graded; reflection text is transient. The related lesson contains the source and shared rubric.
objectives: Define boards, columns, cards, ordering, permissions, and pending mutations.
Draw the component hierarchy and trace a card move through server confirmation to other clients.
Explain conflict handling, reconnect recovery, and keyboard alternatives. Show why rolling back a failed move cannot erase a newer successful change.

prediction.prompt: Which area is most likely to expose a weakness in your first design?

options.label: An uncertain request outcome or recovery gap.
Performance or accessibility under the stated constraints.

steps.title: 0–7 minutes: clarify the scope
steps.instructions: Design a board where users create cards, move them between columns, and see teammates’ changes. Identify two main journeys, required devices, freshness, permissions, and exclusions. Separate requirements from assumptions.

steps.title: 7–20 minutes: draw the architecture
steps.instructions: Draw the component hierarchy and trace a card move through server confirmation to other clients. Assign state owners and component inputs/events. Include loading, empty, and error states.

steps.title: 20–30 minutes: define data and APIs
steps.instructions: Define boards, columns, cards, ordering, permissions, and pending mutations. Specify one read and one write, including identities, response fields, cache policy, and safe retry conditions.

steps.title: 30–45 minutes: trace behavior and recovery
steps.instructions: Trace one interaction from input to confirmed state, then fail a request. Explain conflict handling, reconnect recovery, and keyboard alternatives. Show why rolling back a failed move cannot erase a newer successful change.

steps.title: 45–55 minutes: handle follow-ups
steps.instructions: Two users move the same card. A move succeeds but its response is lost. The board contains thousands of cards. Dragging is unavailable. Pick the hardest case and show which decisions change. State any unresolved limits.

steps.title: 55–60 minutes: review your evidence
steps.instructions: Score scope, components, state and data, APIs and consistency, failure recovery, and quality and trade-offs. Use 0: missing, 1: mentioned, 2: explained with a concrete decision and consequence. Check only evidence you can show. Choose the weakest dimension and redraw it; this is not an employer hiring threshold.

evidenceChecklist.label: I stated the main journeys, assumptions, and exclusions.
I drew component responsibilities and interaction contracts.
I assigned state owners, stable identities, and invariants.
I defined reads, writes, caching, and reconciliation.
I traced one failure through usable recovery.
I defended accessibility, performance, measurement, and alternatives.
I showed that a failed move cannot overwrite a newer confirmed change and provided a keyboard alternative.

reflectionPrompts: Explain conflict handling, reconnect recovery, and keyboard alternatives. Show why rolling back a failed move cannot erase a newer successful change.
Which decision changed after a follow-up, and what requirement caused it?
Which dimension was weakest, and what will you redraw next time?
extensionChallenge: Disconnect one collaborator during concurrent moves, then reconnect. Extend the diagram to distinguish pending intent, confirmed state, and missed events.
